titleEn: Into Your hand I entrust my spirit
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty-five verses that swing between panic and confidence, twice over: the speaker is slandered, besieged, avoided in the street and forgotten like a dead man, and each time the description of the trouble hits bottom he turns and says again that he has taken refuge. Verse 6 is the line most people know before they know the psalm, since its first half is said at bedtime and reworked in the third person in Adon Olam. For a learner the psalm is a drill in the suffix: almost every verb in it carries an object suffix meaning me, and almost every noun a possessive suffix meaning my or Your. Watch the space vocabulary too, because verse 10 says literally that it is tight for the speaker and verse 9 answers with feet set in a wide place.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster.
A psalm of David.

verses.summary: A performance heading, not part of the prayer. It marks the psalm as something handed to a musician rather than a private note.

stichs.en: In You, LORD, I have taken refuge;
let me never be put to shame;
in Your righteousness set me free.

verses.summary: The opening puts the verb in the perfect: the refuge is already taken, before any request is made. What is asked for is only that the choice not turn out to have been humiliating.

stichs.en: Turn Your ear to me, rescue me quickly;
be for me a rock of refuge,
a fortified house, to save me.

verses.summary: Four imperatives in one verse, and the metaphors are all architecture: rock, refuge, fortified house. The speaker is asking to be moved inside something with walls.

stichs.en: For You are my crag and my fortress,
and for Your name's sake You lead me and guide me.

verses.summary: The request of verse 3 is restated as a fact. Note the reason given for the guidance: not the speaker's merit, but the name, which is the same argument Psalm 23 makes at its own turning point.

stichs.en: Bring me out of the net they hid for me,
for You are my stronghold.

verses.summary: The threat becomes concrete for the first time, and it is a trap rather than an army. The enemies here work by concealment, which is why the whole psalm is preoccupied with tongues and whispering.

stichs.en: Into Your hand I entrust my spirit;
You have redeemed me, LORD, God of truth.

verses.summary: The verb is the one used for leaving property with someone for safekeeping. The spirit is deposited, not surrendered, and the second half already speaks of the rescue as finished.

stichs.en: I hate those who keep worthless idols,
but I have trusted in the LORD.

verses.summary: A line of separation. The speaker defines himself against a group before naming what he is for, and the two halves are built to mirror each other verb for verb.

stichs.en: I will exult and rejoice in Your kindness,
for You have seen my affliction,
You have known the troubles of my soul.

verses.summary: The grounds for joy are not that the trouble ended but that it was witnessed. Seeing and knowing are the two verbs, and both are in the perfect.

stichs.en: You have not handed me over to an enemy;
You have set my feet in open ground.

verses.summary: The end of the first movement, and the high point of confidence in the psalm. Rescue is described spatially, as room to stand, which is exactly what the next verse takes away.

stichs.en: Be gracious to me, LORD, for I am in distress;
my eye is wasted with grief,
my soul and my body too.

verses.summary: The psalm restarts from zero. The Hebrew literally says it is tight for me, which is the opposite of the wide place two lines earlier, and the damage is then listed body part by body part.

stichs.en: For my life is spent in sorrow, and my years in sighing;
my strength fails through my guilt,
and my bones waste away.

verses.summary: The one line in the psalm that concedes fault. Everywhere else the trouble comes from outside, and here the speaker names his own guilt as part of what is wearing him down.

stichs.en: Because of all my adversaries I have become a disgrace,
and to my neighbours most of all,
a dread to those who know me;
those who see me in the street run from me.

verses.summary: The circle of rejection tightens from enemies to neighbours to friends. The worst of it is not the adversaries but the people who used to know him crossing the road.

stichs.en: I am forgotten like a dead man, gone from the heart;
I have become like a vessel thrown away.

verses.summary: The lowest point. Social death is described first, then reduced to a household image: a pot that broke and was not worth keeping.

stichs.en: For I have heard the whispering of many,
terror on every side,
as they take counsel together against me,
they plot to take my life.

verses.summary: Rumour turns into conspiracy inside a single verse. The two words for terror on every side are the phrase the book of Jeremiah keeps returning to.

stichs.en: But I have trusted in You, LORD;
I said: You are my God.

verses.summary: The hinge of the second movement, and the same move as verse 7: the opening word sets the speaker apart from the many of the previous line.

stichs.en: My times are in Your hand;
rescue me from my enemies and from those who chase me.

verses.summary: The same phrase as verse 6 opens the line, but what is deposited has changed from the spirit to the timing of events. Two hands are then set against each other in one verse.

stichs.en: Make Your face shine on Your servant;
save me in Your kindness.

verses.summary: The image is borrowed from the priestly blessing. After a verse about hands, the request moves to a face, which is the psalm's word for attention being given.

stichs.en: LORD, let me not be put to shame, for I have called on You;
let the wicked be shamed, silenced down in Sheol.

glosses: let them be put to shame
verses.summary: The verb of verse 2 comes back word for word, now with a second clause attached. The prayer is no longer only for himself, and it is the one place where the psalm asks for something to happen to someone else.

stichs.en: Let lying lips be struck dumb,
that speak insolently against the righteous, with pride and contempt.

verses.summary: The punishment asked for fits the crime exactly: the weapon in this psalm is speech, so what is requested is silence rather than defeat.

stichs.en: How great is Your goodness, stored up for those who fear You,
which You have done for those who take refuge in You, in full view of everyone.

verses.summary: The turn to praise, and the pronoun opens outward: it is no longer me but those who take refuge, the class the speaker joined back in verse 2. The goodness is both hidden away and done in public.

stichs.en: You hide them in the shelter of Your presence from human scheming;
You keep them in a booth from the strife of tongues.

verses.summary: The architecture of verse 3 returns, but softened: not a fortress now, a booth. The threat it protects against is still speech, which no wall would stop anyway.

stichs.en: Blessed is the LORD,
for He made His kindness wondrous to me in a city under siege.

verses.summary: A blessing formula, which usually opens a prayer and here closes one. The setting named is a siege, the one situation in which walls and no room are the same fact.

stichs.en: And I said in my panic: I am cut off from Your sight;
yet You heard my pleas when I cried out to You.

verses.summary: The speaker quotes his own despair and immediately contradicts it. The admission that the panic was wrong is what licenses the two verses of instruction that follow.

stichs.en: Love the LORD, all His faithful ones;
the LORD guards the loyal,
and repays in full measure the one who acts in arrogance.

verses.summary: The first plural imperative in the psalm. Having spent twenty-two verses saying I, the speaker turns and addresses a room, and what he has learned is put as a rule that applies to them.

stichs.en: Be strong, and let your heart take courage,
all you who wait for the LORD.

verses.summary: The psalm ends on an instruction rather than a rescue. Nothing has been reported as resolved; what is offered is a way to stand while it is not.

pardes.body: The psalm says the same thing twice from opposite ends. Verses 2 to 9 run refuge, request, and thanks for a rescue already given, and close at their most confident with feet set in a wide place. Verse 10 then starts again from nothing, and the second lament goes much further down: wasted eyes, failing strength, neighbours crossing the street, a body treated as a broken pot. Verses 15 to 19 repeat the petition almost word for word, and verses 20 to 25 answer it with praise. The last two verses are the real ending, because the grammar changes: after twenty-two verses of I and You, the speaker turns and gives a plural instruction to other people. Nothing in the situation is reported as fixed. What has changed is who is being spoken to.

The psalm is built on a contrast between narrow and wide. Verse 10 does not say I am in distress, it says {{10.3}}, it is tight, and the rescue in the verse before is {{9.5}}, a broad place, room to put your feet down. The siege of {{22.7}} is the same idea made literal: a city with walls is also a city with nowhere to go. Two other threads hold the halves together. The plea not to be put to shame appears in identical form at {{2.4}} and again at {{18.2}}, bracketing everything between them. And {{14.4}} with the word after it, terror on every side, is the phrase the book of Jeremiah uses repeatedly, including as a name given to a man in Jeremiah 20. Which text is drawing on which is not settled, and the psalm carries no date that would settle it.

The first half of verse 6 was lifted out of the psalm and given a nightly job: {{6.0}} and the two words after it are said before sleep, in the reading of the Shema at bedtime, and Adon Olam reworks the same clause into the third person. Read that way, sleep is rehearsal. The verb is the one used for leaving goods with a trusted keeper, so the soul is not given up but deposited, with the expectation of collecting it in the morning. The same phrase opens verse 16, where what is deposited is not the spirit but the timing of a life, which extends the reading from one night to a whole biography. The closing verse also has a near twin: {{25.0}} and what follows it stand in the singular at the end of Psalm 27, the psalm many communities say every day from the start of Elul, so the same encouragement reaches a learner from two directions.

In the mystical reading the deposit of verse 6 is taken literally as the nightly return of the soul to its source, and the morning blessing over the soul restored is its answer. Shelter is the other image the reading works on. Verse 21 puts the protected inside {{21.6}}, a booth, immediately after saying they are hidden in the shelter of the face, and a booth is the standard image for a covering that surrounds rather than a wall that blocks: it is closed on all sides yet open above, so the protection and the exposure are the same structure. Read this way the psalm is not asking for the siege to lift. It is asking for the space inside the siege to be experienced as a shelter, which is why the last word of the psalm is about waiting and not about deliverance.
